## Description

Most research code lives on our laptops in a folder that grows organically over months or years. When the time comes to share it (for a paper, a collaboration, or just our future selves), the folder is hard to clean up and maybe the code does not run anymore.
In this one-hour lecture we look at good practices for reproducible and reusable research code and learn how to improve our own repositories.

We will cover three things:

- **What makes a good repository:** README, license, structure, dependencies, reproducibility, citation metadata.
- **Where and how to publish:** GitHub, Zenodo for archiving and DOI, and the integration between the two.
- **A demo of an AI-assisted repository reviewer** that reads a repository and writes a plain-language report of what to fix before publishing.

The lecture is language agnostic and focuses on data analysis repositories rather than scientific software.

You'll take home a checklist for your own repository, a portable prompt to run a similar audit with your AI tool of choice, and a list of existing tools and references to consult.

## Resources

### General

- [Data- and code-archiving in the British Ecological Society journals](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.70338): Overview of the state of code sharing, tips on how to structure projects and readmes
- [An overview of publications and practical guides](https://research-compendium.science/) to create a research compendium
- [The Turing Way](https://book.the-turing-way.org/): community handbook for reproducible research
- [BES Guide to Reproducible Code](https://bes-guide.github.io/reproducible-code/)
- [Good enough practices in scientific computing](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510)
- [Ten principles for reliable, efficient, and adaptable coding in psychology and cognitive neuroscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-025-00236-3)


### Project structure & file naming

- [rrtools](https://github.com/benmarwick/rrtools) (R) and [computational notebooks](https://github.com/FellowsFreiesWissen/computational_notebooks) (R): research-compendium templates
- [Cookiecutter Data Science](https://cookiecutter-data-science.drivendata.org/) (Python): a project-structure template
- [How to name files](https://speakerdeck.com/jennybc/how-to-name-files): talk by Jenny Bryan

### Running the code: dependencies, workflows, paths

- [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) (R) and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (Python): record and restore project dependencies
- [pipreqs](https://pypi.org/project/pipreqs/): list the packages a Python project actually imports
- [Rocker](https://rocker-project.org/) (Docker images for R) and [repo2docker](https://repo2docker.readthedocs.io/): containers, the last resort when versions alone are not enough
- [targets](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/) (R) and [Snakemake](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) (any language): workflow tools that run steps in the right order and rerun only what changed
- [here](https://here.r-lib.org/) (R) and [pyprojroot](https://pypi.org/project/pyprojroot/) (Python): project-root paths that work on any machine

### Licence & citation

- [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com): pick a licence and copy its text
- [The Turing Way on licensing](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/licensing/)
- [A case for CC0](https://blog.datadryad.org/2023/05/30/good-data-practices-removing-barriers-to-data-reuse-with-cc0-licensing/): by the Dryad repository
- [cffinit](https://citation-file-format.github.io/cff-initializer-javascript/): build a `CITATION.cff` file through a web form

### Archiving & DOIs

- [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org), [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/), [Figshare](https://figshare.com/): repositories that freeze a version and give you a DOI
- [GitHub → Zenodo guide](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content): archive a release and get a DOI
